decision: Persist worker registration and anti-replay state using a locked atomic JSON registry, and require monotonic signed request counters when durable replay protection is enabled

evaluatedApproaches.name: durable-monotonic-counter-per-worker
evaluatedApproaches.correctness: strong restart-safe replay rejection because each authenticated worker request advances one persisted counter
evaluatedApproaches.robustness: survives coordinator restart and rejects duplicate or regressed counters atomically across local coordinator processes
evaluatedApproaches.latency: one serialized registry mutation per authenticated request; higher than memory-only nonce cache but still suitable for lab-scale workers
evaluatedApproaches.resourceUse: low disk footprint; whole-file JSON rewrite is O(worker count)
evaluatedApproaches.regressionRisk: medium because durable mode requires clients to persist and increment counters
evaluatedApproaches.qa: tests cover restart persistence, replay after restart, concurrent duplicate counters, capability spoof prevention, and offline worker rejection

evaluatedApproaches.name: persistent-nonce-set
evaluatedApproaches.correctness: can reject exact replay across restart
evaluatedApproaches.robustness: requires TTL cleanup and potentially unbounded nonce storage under load
evaluatedApproaches.latency: similar or worse due to larger persistent replay set
evaluatedApproaches.regressionRisk: low client change but higher coordinator storage complexity
evaluatedApproaches.qa: rejected in favor of compact monotonic state

evaluatedApproaches.name: memory-only-nonce-cache
evaluatedApproaches.correctness: good only within one coordinator lifetime
evaluatedApproaches.robustness: replay state is lost on restart
evaluatedApproaches.qa: retained only as backwards-compatible LAB fallback when no durable replay store is configured

evaluatedApproaches.name: external-transactional-registry
evaluatedApproaches.correctness: strongest long-term option for multi-VM or multi-host coordination
evaluatedApproaches.robustness: can provide transactional counter acceptance and availability guarantees
evaluatedApproaches.regressionRisk: high before Qubes transport and deployment topology are fixed

whyItWon: It closes the specific coordinator-restart replay gap with minimal persistent state, provides atomic duplicate rejection, binds naturally into the existing HMAC envelope, and lets registered capabilities become coordinator-authoritative instead of worker-self-asserted.
knownFailuresAndLessons: Counter state on the worker side must also be persisted; resetting a worker counter causes safe rejection until it is re-provisioned or explicitly re-enrolled.
The JSON registry is still shared-filesystem LAB infrastructure, not a distributed database.
Whole-file rewrites add per-request I/O and will not scale to high request rates; batch/session reservation or a transactional store is the next performance step.
Registration currently authenticates with the pre-provisioned worker secret; secret issuance and rotation are still external responsibilities.
Coordinator-authoritative capabilities prevent a worker from claiming extra abilities in its request payload, but policy for capability changes still needs explicit operator authorization.
REAL-WORKER readiness still requires a Qubes-safe confidential transport, secret provisioning/rotation, multi-VM partition tests, and idempotency/fencing for external side effects.
